terms.comment: The household word: in the libellī the boy ‘reads’ a book by looking at its pictures, pictūrās spectāvit.
A likeness of someone or something; the lexicon’s photo is imāgō phōtographica.

phrases.latin: Theodōrus librum ā patre accēpit, et ōre clausō, oculīs apertīs, pictūrās spectāvit.
phrases.english: Theo took the book from Dad and, with his mouth shut and his eyes open, looked at the pictures.
phrases.source: Libellus VI, Reditus: per Alpēs domum

phrases.english: he feeds his heart on the empty picture
and, knowing nothing of what it shows, he delights in the picture

pictura.html: Lewis & Short leaves the vowel unmarked, as in pictus and pictor; de Vaan 465 sets Proto-Italic *pikto-, painted. The libellī write pictūrās.

sources: Lewis & Short: pictura · Lewis & Short: imago · Lewis & Short: tabula
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 168, 360. Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. painting; p. 52.
Michiel de Vaan, Etymological Dictionary of Latin and the other Italic Languages (2008), p. 465, s.v. pingō.
Vergil, A. 8.730, from the Latinitas loci collection (loci-vergilius); A. 1.464 as Lewis & Short quotes it (s.v. pāscō).
Theodōrus et pater · Ad Larem avītum, Libellī I–VII, as they stood on 9 November 2026. Examples marked “Libellus” quote those texts word for word.
